    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40584v1</id>
    <title>Early career researcher responses to AI in math</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T17:46:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40584v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40584v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We've heard a lot about AI in math from Fields medalists, AI labs, and established professors. However, the personal stakes are highest for early career researchers. Hoping to provide a platform for graduate students and postdocs to voice their opinions, concerns, and experiences, we wrote and distributed a survey on AI in math.
  In this article, we share the responses to our survey. All responses are anonymous, and respondents came from almost $60$ institutions and at least $5$ countries. Our survey included both multiple choice questions and more open-ended free response questions.
  If you are a senior mathematician or university administrator reading these survey results, our goal is for you to understand the concerns of the younger generations and use your authority to take action accordingly. If you are an early career mathematician reading these survey results, we hope you find comfort in the knowledge that your experiences are shared by many others. If you are not a mathematician, we hope you come away from this article with a deeper understanding of the goals, values, and concerns of the community.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40382v1</id>
    <title>Beyond Selected Breakthroughs: Evaluating Language Models on Randomly Sampled Mathematical Conjectures</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T16:24:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40382v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40382v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The last year has seen a shift in AI-assisted mathematics, with frontier language models producing proofs of and counterexamples to long-standing open conjectures. However, studying only the current set of major breakthroughs provides an incomplete picture of LLM capabilities and the computational resources needed to achieve reported results. To address this, we introduce a new dataset, OpenConjecture, which collects conjectures from mathematics papers published on the arXiv since February 2026. We use these conjectures as a source of open mathematical problems, and apply frontier GPT models to a random sample of 200 of these conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific mathematical guidance. Rather than attempt expert verification of these candidate solutions, we analyze the types of problems for which LLMs produce solutions and the characteristics of these solutions. The models we test produce candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. We estimate solution novelty, assess how solutions cite and relate to existing literature, and analyze whether the proposed resolution relies on either an error in or underspecification of the conjecture. We find that models sometimes propose resolutions that are outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that a number of proofs follow closely from existing results, but that some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty. Our findings underscore the need for evaluations that go beyond correctness to assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39769v1</id>
    <title>The Gleason--Kahane--Zelazko theorem: a gentle introduction</title>
    <updated>2026-10-29T10:20:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39769v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.39769v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>After some personal recollections of Jean-Pierre Kahane, this paper gives a gentle introduction to the Gleason-Kahane-Zelazko theorem. The theorem states that a normalised complex-linear functional on a unital complex Banach algebra is multiplicative whenever it does not vanish on invertible elements. Neither continuity of the functional nor commutativity of the algebra is assumed. We give a detailed account of three proofs: the original argument of Gleason and, independently, Kahane and Zelazko; the polynomial proof of Roitman and Sternfeld; and a proof by the author. We explain the complex analysis behind each: a special case of Hadamard's factorisation theorem, a polynomial argument using the fundamental theorem of algebra, and the Pólya-Saxer theorem on zero-free entire functions and their derivatives. The elementary entire-function lemma needed for the first proof is proved in full; the Pólya-Saxer theorem is used without proof. We give full details of the algebraic argument common to the three proofs, which deduces multiplicativity from the preservation of squares, including the non-commutative case. We then discuss applications and counterexamples, and present an extension to Ransford's generalised spectra using the Roitman--Sternfeld argument. We conclude with a brief guide to the more recent literature.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37260v1</id>
    <title>Mathematical Reality Capture: from the age of discoveries to mathematical topography and surveys</title>
    <updated>2026-10-27T13:55:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37260v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.37260v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A proof answers a precise question, but mathematical understanding also grows through the relationships that its answer makes visible. A point measurement likewise differs from a photograph or a three-dimensional reconstruction of a building. In this work, we argue that, with the help of AI, mathematics should move from a discipline focused on isolated investigations of mathematical objects towards one capable of mapping them systematically. We therefore introduce the idea of "Mathematical Reality Capture", inspired by digital surveying and the reconstruction of a scene from several viewpoints. An elementary example shows how comparing algebra and geometry can illuminate the same phenomenon, provided that we distinguish diversity of explanations from validity of proof. From this analogy we derive criteria for building verifiable atlases, an experiment with which to assess their usefulness, and a reflection on the role of mathematicians in interpreting them.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36300v1</id>
    <title>Building Mathematical Software -- Lessons from the Development of GAP</title>
    <updated>2026-10-26T21:26:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36300v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.36300v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mathematical software has particular needs that are not all covered by the existing literature on software engineering or algorithm design. This paper looks at some of these aspects, in the concrete context of the computer algebra system GAP. It also studies the potential impact AI systems could have on the development process for mathematical software.</summary>
